ACT-RD7-P1-Q1.pick: the booming face is a dry, loosely packed layer lying over a denser, damper bed.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q1.note: Passage A para 2 flags this itself: the geophones were buried ten centimetres to two metres and 'the result that organized everything else was this: the booming face is layered.' D is the one real pull - a solver may reason that only an instrument could yield 'near 90 hertz', and the passage does not say what produced that figure. But para 1 reports 90 Hz from sitting on the crest, before any instrument is named, and the stem asks what the measurements ESTABLISHED, which the text marks explicitly. C is contradicted ('lasts as long as the avalanche does'); B is para 1 procedure. Subject recall: no. Nothing here is available from priors - the 90/layered split is specific to this text.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q2.pick: a decrease in the thickness of the dry surface layer.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q2.note: Para 3: 51 cm in October, 29 in March, 76 Hz to 104. The attribution tag in the stem ('Passage A attributes') is load-bearing and A is the correct Passage B attribution for the same rise, which is the best distractor in the paired set. C is explicitly refused ('No property of the grains changed... the same grains'); D inverts the drying. Subject recall: RECALL-ASSISTED. Option B is the signature claim of the real-world waveguide camp and A the signature claim of the real-world shear-synchronisation camp, so a solver who knows the literature and knows which passage is which can route by camp without reading para 3. The stem still has to tell them which passage, which is what keeps this from being decidable cold.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q3.pick: a grain striking early is slowed and a grain striking late is driven forward.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q3.note: Near-verbatim from Passage B para 2. B (steel floor reflects energy) is a nice trap because it imports Passage A's waveguide mechanism into the chute; C (moisture binding) is Passage A's damp bed; D (sorting by diameter) is invented but reads well against 'fixed by the shear rate and the grain diameter'. Subject recall: no - the entrainment sentence is this text's wording and none of the distractors is refuted by priors alone.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q4.pick: booming does not require the layered structure that Passage A describes.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q4.note: Para 1 is built to make exactly this point: 'There is no damp bed under a dry layer; there are eight centimetres of poured sand on a steel floor', and it booms at 95 Hz. D is the only one worth a second look - a reader may take 'two metres long' and 'no dune in the chute' as concessions of inadequacy - but Passage B offers the chute as decisive, not as limited, so nothing in it implies the chute is too short. Subject recall: YES, RECALL-DECISIVE. With both passages covered I would still pick C from priors: 'sand booms in a lab chute, therefore the dune's layering is not necessary' is the actual published argument against the waveguide account, and no other option is a claim anyone makes about booming sand. This is the weakest item in the paired set on the recall axis.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q5.pick: A thinner dry layer avalanches faster, so the shear rate changed as well.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q5.note: Passage B para 3 states it outright: the crust weakens as the sand dries, a thinner dry layer avalanches faster, so shear rate should also climb by March - the confound is what makes the field result compatible with both accounts. A is Passage A's own sentence repurposed, which is the right kind of trap. Labelled hard; I score it medium, because B para 3 supplies the answer in one sentence and C is the only option that names a second variable at all. Subject recall: RECALL-ASSISTED - the coupling-of-the-two-quantities objection is the real dispute's standard move, and C is the only option shaped like it.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q6.pick: allowing no excuse if it turns out to be wrong.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q6.note: Checked the span: 'unforgiving' occurs exactly once in Passage A, para 3, modifying 'The prediction that follows', and the next sentence gives the sense - 'If the layer sets the note, the note must move when the layer does', i.e. the prediction leaves no room to retreat if the note does not move. B is the strongest distractor in the batch: 'unforgiving' in its everyday sense fits terrain and labour, and this passage really does describe two trenches cut across a dune face five months apart, so a solver who fixes on the fieldwork rather than the referent ('the prediction') lands on B. A and C attach the word to people instead of to the claim. Genuinely hard, and hard for the right reason. Subject recall: no.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q7.pick: accepting the measurement but denying that it separates the two accounts.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q7.note: Passage B para 3 opens 'We take the trench measurement seriously and we do not think it is a mistake. We think it is ambiguous', and closes 'it was collected in the one place where the two cannot be told apart.' D is the reflex answer for anyone who assumes a rival must reject the data, and A imports the grain account Passage B never makes. Labelled medium; it is easy, because the key is a two-clause paraphrase of two adjacent sentences. Subject recall: no.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q8.pick: it grants that without an avalanche there is no energy to guide.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q8.note: Passage A para 4: 'We do not say the avalanche is unimportant. Without one there is no energy to guide' - the avalanche is exactly what Passage B says sets the note, so this is the anticipation. Exclusive, but the item is weaker than its label. The other three options describe concessions Passage A never makes anywhere: it mentions two-metre geophone depth as a fact, not a limit; it never calls six seasons short; it never calls the February silence unexplained (it attributes it to rain). So the item is decidable by absence - scan A for anything that reads as a concession, find one, stop - which collapses a cross-passage task into a locate-the-detail task and is why I score it medium rather than hard. The fix, if the batch is revised, is to make one or two distractors point at real sentences in Passage A that are simply not concessions to Passage B's objection. Subject recall: no.

ACT-RD7-P1-Q9.pick: Sound is produced only while an avalanche is in motion.
ACT-RD7-P1-Q9.note: Passage A: 'It lasts as long as the avalanche does.' Passage B locates the sound in an actively shearing layer, which on a dune face is the avalanche. D is the cleanest elimination - Passage A would accept it and Passage B is written specifically to deny it (no damp bed, still booms). B and C are shared by neither. One softness worth recording: Passage B never makes a duration claim in its own voice, so agreement with the key is inferred from the chute description rather than stated, and a pedant could observe that B's chute booms with no avalanche at all; the stem's restriction to 'a booming dune' is what closes that off, and it does close it. I would not spend the drop vote here, but the stem is carrying more weight than it looks. Subject recall: YES, RECALL-DECISIVE. With both passages covered I would pick A from priors - sustained avalanching is the known precondition for booming and the other three 'only while' frames are each false in the real world. Note the option set is otherwise well built: four parallel 'Sound is produced only while X' frames varying only in X, which is the CLEAN shape under the options-only rule, so the leak here is subject recall and not option shape.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q1.pick: whose ordinary effort the standard is measured against.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q1.note: Para 2 ends 'The rulebook says ordinary effort. It does not say whose ordinary.' The item is a direct restatement and para 7 pays it off ('ninety shortstops in a hundred do not reach'). C is the best distractor because para 6 does raise a not-seeing-clearly theme, but that is about the narrator's memory of choosing, not about the rulebook's silence; A and B are not in the text.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q2.pick: an account of how things already stand.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q2.note: Checked the reference: 'description' occurs exactly once in the passage and it is in paragraph 3 as shipped, so the paragraph citation is accurate. The sentence sets the contrast itself - 'He meant it as instruction. I took it as description, which is how a person mistakes a wish for a fact' - so description is the is-side of an is/ought pair. A is a strong distractor because it is precisely the sense the father intended and a hurried reader will take the father's meaning as the passage's; B is the everyday sense of 'description'; D is the taxonomic sense. The word 'fact' at the end of the same sentence is what keeps this medium rather than hard.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q3.pick: reached a judgment on the play and knew it was not theirs to enter.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q3.note: Para 5: 'Four hundred people ruled on the play in the same half second and then remembered that the ruling was not theirs' - the key's two clauses map onto the sentence's two clauses. B is genuinely tempting and I considered dropping the item for it: 'What came out of the crowd was not a groan and not a cheer' can be read as a divided crowd making two sounds at once. It does not survive the next sentence, which has all four hundred ruling together and the neither-groan-nor-cheer explained by self-restraint rather than by disagreement. Exclusive, but by one sentence.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q4.pick: supply the standard against which she later measures her own ruling.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q4.note: The father's saying is invoked twice at the decisive moments - para 6 ('my father would have said reaching is not catching') and para 8 ('my father's saying is true in a way he did not intend') - so its function is to set the measure. D is the only distractor with a foothold, via the ruled index cards, but the cards mark a CHANGE in how the book was kept (his hand-ruled cards, her league scorebook in a bank bag), so it inverts the detail it leans on. B is contradicted; A is never discussed.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q5.pick: was managing her awareness of an outcome she preferred.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q5.note: Checked the span: 'did not look up at the press-box window' appears verbatim once, in paragraph 6. The inference chain is the longest in the batch and the item earns its label - the sentence says only that not looking was 'a decision... made very deliberately, which is not what a person does who wants nothing', and the wanting is not named until para 8 ('I had wanted Ronan to have his game'). D is contradicted by 'The pencil had already written something'; C invents an expectation of dispute; A is refused by the whole quiet-in-the-stands paragraph. The one reservation is that the key's phrasing ('managing her awareness') is a shade more clinical than anything the narrator says, but no other option is defensible.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q6.pick: It entered as a failure a play that few shortstops would have reached.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q6.note: Para 7: 'She had reached a ball that ninety shortstops in a hundred do not reach, and the book said that she had failed' - ten in a hundred is 'few'. C is the strong one and the right kind of trap: the Herald-Sentinel did run a 1 under E the next morning, so the sentence is half true, but a line score carries no fielder's name and the passage never says her name appeared. B is the plausible-consequence invention (she stops speaking to the narrator, but nothing about her place on the team); D reverses her position.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q7.pick: acceptance of it on grounds he did not intend.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q7.note: Para 8: 'my father's saying is true in a way he did not intend', then the reconstructed grounds - not that the scorer has no wants, but that admitting them converts the record into an opinion. A is the good distractor because it is the same acceptance minus the reinterpretation, and it takes the para 3 instruction/description contrast to see that the difference matters; C and D both require a rejection the text never makes. Close to easy given how explicit the key sentence is; I keep it medium because A and B are separated only by the qualifier.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q8.pick: is recalling, long afterward, an episode she has not settled for herself.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q8.note: Both halves are anchored: distance ('I used to find comforting', 'I have thought since', 'I gave the bag back in August') and unsettledness ('I have never been sure whether that is why I wrote what I wrote'). C is the best distractor and rests on a real sentence - people in the IGA told her she had gotten it right for a week - but being told is not being shown, and the closing paragraph refuses the settlement outright. A misreads the retrospective frame; B invents second-hand sourcing when the whole account is first-hand. Labelled hard; medium, because the final paragraph states the unsettledness in so many words.

ACT-RD7-P2-Q9.pick: turn the book from a record into an opinion that has to be weighed.
ACT-RD7-P2-Q9.note: Checked the reference: the final paragraph is paragraph 8 as shipped, and the key is a near-verbatim compression of one sentence in it - 'the book stops being a record and becomes an opinion with her name on it, and everyone who reads it, herself included, has to weigh it.' Exclusive and correct, but labelled hard and it is easy: the stem points at one paragraph, that paragraph contains one conditional, and the key repeats its two nouns. A is the only distractor with any pull (consistency across games is a plausible worry the text never raises); C and D are outside the passage. If the batch needs a genuinely hard closer, this is the item to rebuild - the abstraction of the idea is doing none of the work because the sentence is right there.
